newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Quality of EMU budget pact still paramount -Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Quality of EMU budget pact still paramount -Waigel.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, now the main obstacle to the creation of a European budget pact he proposed, made clear on Monday that he would not make overly generous concessions to secure a deal by year-end.

Briefing journalists after the European Union's ECOFIN council postponed agreeing terms for the so-called stability pact on budget discipline, Waigel said Germany had shown some flexibility in the talks but would not drop all of its demands.
"It would be desirable if we could succeed in securing an agreement before Dublin," he said, referring to next week's summit meeting in the Irish city. "But not at any cost."

"Of course it would be nice if it could be agreed as soon as possible. On the other hand we are not under time pressure. The important thing is to agree something which is appropriate, sensible and acceptable and we must take the time for that."

Waigel, who proposed the pact to reassure a sceptical German public that the planned single currency will not be undermined by lax fiscal policies in Europe, has maintained throughout that the agreement can only be effective if it has teeth.

But most other European ministers have baulked at Germany's wish to set strict numerical limits on the exceptional economic circumstances which could allow a country's deficit to exceed the agreed maximum of three percent of gross domestic product.
Their objections have succeeded only in making Germany even more wary of a looser deal, open to political interpretation.

Playing a new tactical card, German officials made clear that a deal on the stability pact must be part of a single package with two other issues on the Dublin agenda, effectively threatening to hold up these matters if no deal was reached.
The other issues concern the exchange rate mechanism to link currencies not in EMU with the new euro -- the so-called EMS 2 -- and the legal framework for the introduction of the euro.

"All three parts hang together both politically and in their subject matter, so that there is only room for an agreement when there is agreement on all three elements," Juergen Stark, state secretary to the German finance ministry, told reporters.

Yet despite the problems in reaching consensus in Brussels, Waigel remained optimistic that common ground could be found, possibly at a newly-convened meeting of finance ministers to be held on December 12 in Dublin, on the eve of the summit.

"In 7-1/2 years as Germany's finance minister...I have experienced so many problems which could be resolved that I am ...neither pessimistic nor depressed, but am rather garnering the courage to go on. Some things take time," he said.
Although he signalled that Germany had made some concessions in the talks, Waigel declined to dwell on these in detail.
"We have made proposals here, we showed flexibility. But there are two or three figures in our proposal where we did not manaage to gain a final agreement," he said.

It was clear that Bonn had softened, but not abandoned, its demands in two key areas where agreement is still outstanding -- the definition of exceptional circumstances which would allow budget excess and the fines offending countries will face.

Germany had come to Brussels seeking a very tough definition of the "exceptional and temporary" economic circumstances which would allow a country to let its budget deficit exceed the set maximum of three percent of GDP.
Under the German plan, an economy would have to contract for four consecutive quarters, or by two percent within a year, for this exception to apply.
Diplomats said this had been cut back in discussions to a 1.5 percent shrinkage over the year.

Germany also dropped its hardline demand for the fine incurred by an offender to kick off at 0.25 percent on GDP, instead accepting a 0.2 percent fine for the initial breach of the three percent level, rising to a maximum of 0.5 percent.
"If it should be 0.2 percent, and if there is agreement on all other issues, we would not block this point," Waigel said.
